parent.name: Queen's Gambit Accepted
parent.overview: After 2...dxc4 Black has taken the c-pawn, but sources agree he cannot keep it without serious concessions; White regains it with Bxc4 once the e-pawn has moved (3.e3 or 3.Nf3 then e3, or 3.e4). Black instead gives up the idea of holding it and fights for central counterplay: ...c5 (and ...cxd4) or ...e5 to undermine d4, and ...a6 with ...b5 to gain queenside space and time for the c8 bishop. The centre is open, White has the d4/e4 pawns and the move, and the usual middlegames are IQP or hanging-pawn positions with piece play. Character varies by line: the 3.Nf3 Nf6 4.e3 e6 5.Bxc4 c5 main line is positional and balanced, while 3.e4 lines can be tactical early. It is sound and has been a regular at the elite level since the 1990s.

parent.name: Queen's Gambit Declined: Three Knights Variation
parent.moves: 1. d4 Nf6 2. c4 e6 3. Nf3 d5 4. Nc3
parent.overview: After 4.Nc3 (reached from 3.Nf3 or 3.Nc3) both sides have developed two pieces and the centre is still in tension; neither has committed. White keeps a choice of 5.Bg5 (the classical Orthodox set-ups), 5.cxd5 (Exchange structures with a Carlsbad pawn structure), 5.e3 (quieter) or Bf4, and Black's 4th move (...Be7, ...Bb4 Ragozin, ...Nbd7 Cambridge Springs set-up) picks the structure. In the main Orthodox lines White pins or pressures the f6 knight and tries to exploit Black's passive light-squared bishop behind e6; Black aims to complete development, castle, and free the position with ...c5, ...e5 or ...dxc4 plus ...b6/...Bb7. The game is usually slow and manoeuvring with the d4/d5 pawns holding the centre; wins come from small structural or space edges rather than early tactics. At 2500 level draws spike (11.7 percent in the Chessiverse data), and it is regarded as one of Black's most reliable replies to 1.d4.

parent.name: Scotch Game
parent.moves: 1. e4 e5 2. Nf3 Nc6 3. d4 exd4 4. Nxd4
parent.overview: White strikes at the centre on move three and, after 3...exd4 4.Nxd4, trades the d-pawn for Black's e-pawn, opening the position early and releasing the central tension (s2). White gets space and quick development, Black gets easy piece play and the choice between active set-ups: 4...Bc5 (Classical), 4...Nf6 (Schmidt) and, less often, 4...Qh4 (Steinitz). The structure is open from the outset, so the game turns on piece activity rather than pawn manoeuvring. It can be played either positionally or tactically depending on the line (s2, s3). Objectively roughly equal: the Classical and Schmidt lines give Black good chances of equality, while Mieses (5.Nxc6 bxc6 6.e5) and the Steinitz are sharper (s1). Kasparov revived it in the 1990s as a way of avoiding the heavy Ruy Lopez theory, and Carlsen, Kramnik and Aronian have used it since (s1, s2, s3).

parent.name: Sicilian Defense: Modern Variations
parent.overview: 2...d6 is a crossroads, not a single set-up. It is the move order that leads to the Najdorf, Dragon, Scheveningen and Classical/Richter-Rauzer after 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 Nf6 5.Nc3 (s4). The open Sicilian is open and extremely complex: White has a lead in development and extra kingside space, Black has a central pawn majority and the open c-file (s1). White often castles queenside against Black's queenside counterplay, giving opposite-side attacks (Yugoslav Attack, English Attack) (s1). 2...d6 also keeps ...d5 off for a move, which is why White has quieter tries here: 3.Bc4, 3.Nc3 and 3.d3 or the Alapin-like 3.d4 cxd4 4.c3 (Tartakower, in the subtree) (s3). The root is described as combative and unbalanced (s2), but how sharp a game is depends heavily on whether White plays 3.d4 or an anti-Sicilian.

parent.name: Petrov's Defense
parent.overview: Black answers 2.Nf3 by counter-attacking e4 rather than defending e5. After 3.Nxe5 d6 4.Nf3 Nxe4 5.d4 d5 6.Bd3 both sides have lost an e-pawn and the structure is symmetrical, with the e-file the main open line. Black's aim is to equalise by quick development and piece trades; White tries to turn a small lead in development or slightly freer play into pressure, often castling and using the e-file or a queenside castling and pawn storm. The 3.d4 Steinitz line (3...Nxe4 4.Bd3 d5 5.Nxe5 Nd7) and 3.Nc3 (Four Knights transposition) or 3.d3 sidelines give quieter or more varied structures. The main lines are widely played at the top and are known as drawish, though some lines hold real attacking chances for both sides.

parent.name: French Defense
parent.overview: Black plays ...e6 and ...d5, accepting a pawn chain and a space deficit in return for a sound position, and then hits White's pawn centre at its base with ...c5. The fight is over the dark squares d4 and e5. Black's problem piece is the light-squared bishop on c8, hemmed in by the e6 pawn; Black solves it by exchanging it or rerouting it (...b6 and ...Ba6, or ...Bd7 with ...Bb5/a4). White typically uses extra space for a kingside attack (f4-f5, and in the Advance the g4/h4 ideas) or expands on the queenside with a3-b4. Play is slower and manoeuvring, with a lot of pawn-break play. It has a reputation for solidity but a cramped early game for Black. The Winawer (3.Nc3 Bb4) is the sharpest branch, the Advance is the main fight in a locked centre, and the Tarrasch, Classical and Exchange are quieter. The root is one position after 1...e6 2.d4 d5; the structures differ strongly by branch.

parent.name: Caro-Kann Defense
parent.overview: Black plays ...c6 to support ...d5 and so challenges the e4 pawn with a sound pawn structure, while keeping the light-squared bishop free to come out to f5 or g4 before ...e6 (the French Defence's main drawback, at the cost of a tempo). Black accepts less space early and tends to get a resilient, hard-to-break structure with few weaknesses and good endgame prospects. Play is mostly positional and manoeuvring; it is called more solid and less dynamic than the Sicilian (s1). The Advance (3.e5 Bf5) and Panov-Botvinnik (3.exd5 cxd5 4.c4) lines are more combative, and the Advance became the most popular White try in the 21st century. Main branches: Classical (4...Bf5), Advance, Exchange, Panov, 4...Nf6 lines, Gurgenidze (...g6), Two Knights (2.Nc3 d5 3.Nf3) and Fantasy (3.f3). This is a crossroads root after 1...c6; the pawn structures differ by branch.

parent.name: Alekhine Defense
parent.overview: Black attacks e4 at once with 1...Nf6 and, after 2.e5 Nd5, invites White to build a broad centre with c4, d4 and perhaps f4, planning to attack that centre later with ...d6, ...Nb6, ...Bg4, ...c5 and ...dxe5. White's job is to keep or use the extra space, either with the most ambitious Four Pawns Attack (4.c4 Nb6 5.f4), the popular Modern Variation 4.Nf3, or the less forcing Exchange 5.exd6; 2.Nc3 avoids the main line entirely. Positions lose symmetry from the start and are unbalanced, with a space edge for White against Black's counterplay on the overextended pawns. The opening is regarded as sound, original and tricky but risky (moderate to high), and is only moderately common at the top: Fischer, Korchnoi, Ivanchuk and occasionally Carlsen have played it.

parent.name: Sicilian Defense: Open
parent.moves: 1. e4 c5 2. Nf3 Nc6 3. d4 cxd4 4. Nxd4 Nf6
parent.overview: After 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 Black has developed the knight to c6 before choosing a set-up, so the root is a crossroads: Classical (5.Nc3 d6), Sveshnikov (5...e5 after ...Nf6), Four Knights (5...e6), Kalashnikov or Lowenthal (4...e5), Accelerated Dragon (4...g6) and Taimanov-type lines (s1, s2, s3). White gets a development lead and kingside space, Black gets the open c-file and a central pawn majority, so the play is unbalanced and complex (s1). The Richter-Rauzer (6.Bg5) and Sozin (6.Bc4) lead to a race where White attacks on the kingside, often castling queenside, and Black counters with ...a6, ...b5 and c-file pressure (s2). Statistics are balanced (White 47.7%, Black 47.3% in 5.6 million Lichess games, per the Chessiverse page for the Four Knights) (s3).

parent.overview: 3...a6 is the main road of the Ruy Lopez (roughly two thirds to 90 per cent of Ruy games per the sources). It asks White's bishop an immediate question: Bxc6 (Exchange) or the retreat 4.Ba4, after which Black can play ...b5 to kick the bishop again. The main line is the Closed Ruy (5.O-O Be7 6.Re1 b5 7.Bb3 d6 8.c3 O-O 9.h3), a locked, slow centre where White builds the c3-d4 pawn duo and reroutes the knight Nb1-d2-f1-g3, and Black seeks queenside counterplay with ...c5/...c4 or ...Bb7 and ...Re8/...Bf8. Alternatives at move five or later include the Open Variation (5...Nxe4), the Arkhangelsk (5...b5), and Marshall Attack (8...d5), with Anti-Marshall systems used by White to dodge it. Play is typically slow positional manoeuvring (the 'Spanish torture': a small White edge pressed for forty moves) with very deep theory. It has been a main weapon of nearly every world champion.
